title: Bainite transformation behavior, microstructural feature and mechanical properties of nanostructured bainitic steel subjected to ausforming with different strain
abstract: The interplay between ausforming strain level applied prior to austempering step and bainite transformation kinetic as well as plastic deformation mechanism of nanostructured bainitic steel was essentially investigated. The results indicated that the bainite transformation proceeded rapidly with increasing ausforming strain owing to the added heterogeneous nucleation sites and overall storage energy. Nevertheless, when the ausforming strain further increased to 40%, the acceleration effect became less pronounced attributing to the counteraction mechanism by inhibition effect of retarded bainite growth. Increasing ausforming strain could effectively refine bainite sheaves and minimize the dimension of blocky retained austenite, yet strengthen undercooled austenite, leading to a decreased volume fraction of bainitic ferrite at the termination of transformation. Ausforming strain had a positive effect on mechanical properties, particularly, the sample ausformed at 300 °C for 40% strain achieved the largest tensile strength of 1900 MPa and the best total elongation of 24%. This enhanced strength–ductility synergy mainly ascribed to the benefit of the refined bainitic ferrite lath and the increased dislocation density together with transformation induced plasticity effect. Unfortunately, the apparent variant selection brought about by ausforming could offset the increased impact toughness resulting from microstructure refinement when ausforming strain was higher than 10%, which leaded to an intensive deterioration of impact property.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: A new generation of nanostructured bainitic steel, developed by Caballero and Bhadeshia  [1,2] , has attracted extensive attention by dint of high strength and excellent ductility coupled with acceptable wear resistance. Owing to the unique comprehensive mechanical performance, nanostructured bainitic steel has shown immense potential in defense applications, offshore structures and automotive crash applications  [3–5] .

Unsatisfactorily, it generally takes as long as a dozen hours or even several days for the completion of bainite transformation at low temperature ranging from 200 °C to 350 °C to obtain a nanostructured microstructure  [6,7] , and the incomplete transformation would drastically compromise the desired comprehensive mechanical properties of material. Furthermore, another aspect that cannot be ignored is the processing technology of nanostructured bainitic steel, which cannot be formed via traditional methods on account of its ultrahigh strength. The matters as mentioned above have hitherto become obstacles in the wide application of nanostructured bainitic steel. Accordingly, a processing method to shorten technological time and maintain high mechanical properties in nanostructured bainitic steel is believed to the primary issue in achieving industrial-scale production.

Ausforming treatment is known to bring about a certain degree of mechanical stabilization of undercooled austenite and significantly influence morphological characteristics, which has been proved to exert a great impact on subsequent martensite and bainite reaction kinetics  [8–16] . Nowadays some ausforming routes have been extensively performed to explore the transformation mechanism. Nonetheless, there is still contradiction in some way concerning the effect of ausforming on bainite transformation due to the different experimental conditions, and the basic standpoints can be roughly divided into three aspects. Ausforming leads to an intensive mechanical stabilization of undercooled austenite and thus restrains subsequent overall bainite transformation  [8–10] ; ausforming introduces heterogeneous nucleation sites, which accelerates the initial stage of bainite transformation, but eventually suppresses bainite growth in the final stage due to work hardening of austenite  [11,12] ; the whole bainite transformation can be promoted by small amount of ausforming at low temperature  [13,9–16] . Therefore, the aim of this work presented in this article is to systematically understand the influence of ausforming strain on phase transformation behavior, to resolve the debate and select optimum ausforming parameters in order to accelerate isothermal bainite transformation.

The majority of previous experimental studies primarily deal with phase transformation mechanism, however, the mechanical properties upon ausforming process have received much less attention. For instance, Zhao et al.  [17]  suggested that ausrolling at 500 °C and austempering at 200 °C could offer not only unique tensile strength but also excellent ductility owing to the increased dislocation density. He et al.  [18]  declared that the bainite transformation rate and tensile properties of high-carbon bainitic steel would be both enhanced by multi-step ausforming. However, Golchin et al.  [19]  reported that 10% ausforming combined with austempering for 6 h or 16 h could achieve high strength at the expensive of impact toughness. Therefore, there also arises a need to systematically evaluate the mechanical properties prepared by ausforming treatment and explore an effective approach to produce nanostructured bainitic steel.

The results of ausforming temperatures on mechanical performances in nanostructured bainitic steel have been analyzed and the corresponding values have been published  [20] . However, in order to obtain optimum ausforming parameters and bear in mind possible problems that may come up when subjects to ausforming treatment, some detailed experiments with regard to ausforming strain need conducting. In this regard, ausforming strains varying from 10% to 40% were conducted to systematically investigate the formed bainitic ferrite from plastically deformed austenite and its effect on transformation kinetics and crystallography characteristics as well as the microstructure-properties relationship.

sections.heading: Material and methods
paragraphs:
The chemical composition of this investigated high-carbon silicon-rich steel was Fe–0.70C–2.47Si-1.46Mn–0.87Al–0.02Nb (all in wt.%). A large amount of Si and Al was added to avoid cementite formation during bainite transformation  [21] . Inclusion of Nb can provide grain refinement by formation of NbC/Nb(CN) precipitate  [22] . A 50 kg ingot was cast in a vacuum induction furnace. The cast steel was forged into square bars and subsequently homogenized at 1200 °C for 36 h. Ausforming treatments were performed on a Gleeble 3500 thermomechanical simulator using cylindrical samples in the form of 6 mm diameter and 10 mm length, to quantitatively evaluate the bainite transformation behavior based on the schematic diagram illustrated in  Fig. 1 
                      . The as-received samples were initially austenitized at 950 °C for 10 min, followed by quenching to 300 °C at a cooling rate of approximately 15 °C/s to prevent the formation of diffusive products and then kept for 1 min at 300 °C, the time which was verified experimentally that bainite transformation had not taken place, to reach a homogeneous temperature throughout the samples. Subsequently, the quenched samples were conducted at 300 °C for various amounts of deformation (10, 20, 30 and 40%) at a strain rate of 5 s −1 , respectively, followed by thermally treating at 300 °C for 4 h to complete bainite transformation. A non-ausforming sample was prepared with same processing procedure to have a reasonable comparison. The change in length as a function of temperature in radial direction performed to cylindrical specimens was recorded simultaneously all over the whole range of heating and holding routes by a laser extensometer involved in each treatment.

Since the low-sized sample for thermomechanical simulation seems not be able to prepare tensile and impact specimens, it is necessary to adopt warm rolling processes instead of compression tests to characterize the mechanical properties. Samples used for warm rolling tests were machined into plates with dimension of 200 mm × 60 mm × 5 mm and 60 mm × 40 mm × 15 mm, respectively. Firstly, the austenitized samples were quenched to molten salt bath furnace and held at 300 °C for 30 s prior to warm rolling to eliminate thermal gradients, and rapidly warm rolled to 10%, 20%, 30% and 40% thickness reduction through a single pass rolling with a two-high mill, respectively. Subsequently the rolled samples were immediately transferred into salt bath furnace to perform isothermal heat treatment at 300 °C for the selected time, which refers to the completion time obtained by thermomechanical simulation test, finally water-cooled to room temperature.

Microstructural observations were performed at central area of the warm rolling specimen along longitudinal section by means of optical microscope (OM, ZEISS AX10), scanning electron microscope (SEM, ZEISS ULTRA 55) and transmission electron microscope (TEM, Tecnai G2 F30S-TWIN). The final balance of phase volume fraction in each condition was calculated from X-ray diffraction pattern (XRD, Bruker D8 DAVINCI, Cu-Kα radiation, scan range: 47−93°, step size: 0.01°). Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) examinations were carried out to investigate crystallographic orientation distribution. Specimens for XRD and EBSD were mechanically ground and electrolytically polished with 25% perchloric acid and 75% ethanol at 25 V for 20 s.

Tensile specimens, with gauge length of 25 mm and thickness of about 2 mm, were extracted from the mid-radius position of the warm-rolled plate along the rolling direction. The tensile tests were conducted on a MTS 810 servohydraulic tensile testing machine with a crosshead speed of 1 mm/min. Stress-strain curves of all specimens were acquired from the tensile test, and the yield stress was determined by the 0.2% offset method. Charpy impact tests were performed using 10 mm × 10 mm × 55 mm U-notched samples on a 300J Charpy testing machine. Microhardness measurements were conducted on a Vickers hardness tester with a load of 10 kgf for 15 s. Tensile, impact and hardness tests were implemented by using multiple samples, respectively, afterward, the mean values were taken to represent the mechanical properties of the tested specimens. The fractographic feature of tensile and impact fracture surface was examined by SEM.

sections.heading: Results
paragraphs:
The dilatation versus time curves of various samples subjected to different processes are plotted in  Fig. 2 
                      a. Due to the unequal initial deformation upon different ausforming conditions, the dilatation of various samples was normalized by dividing the diameter change during austempering (Δd) by the initial diameter after deformation (d 0 ). Generally speaking, the time at which obtains the explosive expansion and utmost expansion from starting point of isothermal holding is respectively taken as the incubation period and completion time of transformation  [20] , that is, 1% and 99% maximum attainment dilatometric date, and the corresponding results are depicted in  Fig. 2 a. As observed in the curves, the incubation stage and completion time of phase transformation from austenite to bainite become significantly shortened with ausforming and varied as changing ausforming strain. When ausforming strain increases from 0 to 30%, the incubation period and completion time of bainite transformation are gradually diminished. For instance, the onset time required for bainite nucleation of applying 30% strain is just approximately 20 s, which is nearly two orders of magnitude lower than non-ausforming sample. Whereas, with the ausforming strain further increases up to 40%, the incubation time and completion time are extended to the same level as 10% strain.

Fig. 2 b shows the corresponding dilatation rate as a function of time (curves) under different ausforming strain.s Obviously, the maximum transformation rates of ausforming samples are higher than that of non-ausforming sample. Whilst the ausforming strain does not exceed 30%, not only can the maximum transformation rate increase with the increase of ausforming strain, but also the time corresponding to the peak rate appears early, which means that the bainite growth rate is accelerated at the early stage of phase transformation. In contrast, as ausforming strain reaches to 40%, the maximum rate of bainite reaction is marginally slowed down and nearly the same as 10% strain.

As a result, it is concluded that the plastic deformation of undercooled austenite at 300 °C can extremely promote isothermal bainite transformation, and the acceleration action will be improved by increasing ausforming strain. Nevertheless, when the ausforming strain is more than 30%, the acceleration effect seems to be weakened.

The OM, SEM and TEM micrographs of different samples isothermally held at 300 °C under various ausforming strain levels are presented in  Fig. 3 
                      , meanwhile the rolling and normal directions are also presented. It is noticed that the microstructures of all samples are composed of lamellar bainite sheaves and blocky retained austenite trapped between different crystallographic variants of bainite sheaves, in which the bright contrast and dark contrast regions in TEM micrograph belong to bainitic ferrite and filmy retained austenite phase in conjunction with an intensive distribution of curved and tangled dislocation, respectively. Clearly, ausforming samples exhibit slightly different structures, and with increasing ausforming strain, the microstructural feature evolves from the initial equiaxial grain structure toward into a pancake-like shape. Meanwhile, it is also worth mentioning that the crystallographic directions of bainite laths in non-ausforming sample are distributed randomly, by contrast, most of bainite sheaves in ausforming samples become more highly ordered and tend to be arranged in limited spatial directions, which are roughly distributed along ±45° with applied strain, in agreement with the previous results reported by Gong et al.  [13] . Furthermore, the bainite sheaves in ausforming samples appear to be fragmented, especially for the higher strain level of 30% and 40% ( Fig. 3 d and e).

The measured average thicknesses of bainitic ferrite lath and filmy retained austenite as well as average size of blocky retained austenite are presented in  Fig. 4 
                      . Thereinto, the average thicknesses of bainitic ferrite lath are determined by mean linear intercept method from image analysis results of a large number of TEM and SEM micrographs and revised by multiplying by 2/π  [23] . Microstructural evaluation confirms that the average lath thicknesses of bainite plate and filmy retained austenite obtained in ausforming samples are all in the scales of tens of nanometers and appear to be evidently thinner and shorter than that in non-ausforming counterparts, and the values gradually decline with increasing in ausforming strain, which is consistent with the observation by Zhang et al.  [15] . Additionally, the quantitative measurement demonstrates that the dimension of blocky retained austenite shows the same trend with bainite lath, which is gradually declined with an increase in ausforming strain and decomposed into dispersed fine particles. In non-ausforming sample, a large region of blocky retained austenite with an average size exceeding 1.2 μm can be observed, whereas the values in ausforming sample for 30% strain are almost lower than 0.3 μm. These outcomes reveal that ausforming process can greatly decrease the quantity and dimension of blocky retained austenite and improve the proportion of filmy retained austenite.

Fig. 5 
                      a shows the XRD patterns of different samples. Evidently, the XRD spectrums obtained from various ausforming processes all contain two kinds of phase diffraction peaks, i.e., BCC ferrite (α) and FCC austenite (γ) peaks, which can be also approved by the TEM observation shown in  Fig. 3 . The corresponding percentages of retained austenite and combined fraction of bainitic ferrite are plotted in  Fig. 5 b. It is clear that ausforming samples generally give rise to a comparatively higher volume fraction of retained austenite relative to non-ausforming sample, and the amount of bainitic ferrite changes nonlinearly with ausforming strain, which exhibits a slight decline trend after an initial ascent.

Fig. 6 
                       shows the EBSD micrographs of bainite formed in various samples. The different colors correspond to different crystallographic orientations normal to the observed plane and stand for various bainitic ferrite variants. It can be recognized that there is a drastic discrepancy between various samples and ausforming strain shows a significant change in variant selection of bainite lath. In non-ausforming sample, approximately 12 different kinds of crystallographic variants can be detected in an individual austenite grain, which is the same with previous reports  [14] . However, for all ausforming treatments, the number of bainite variants seems to be significantly reduced, only 7, 5, 4 and 4 kinds of variants are respectively found in ausforming sample for 10%, 20%, 30% and 40% strain within a single austenite grain. Therefore, ausforming contributes to the distribution of crystallographic orientations in bainite sheaves, and this phenomenon is more pronounced upon higher ausforming strain level where the orientation of bainite sheaves becomes narrower corresponding to the rolling direction. Previous studies have also proven that ausforming at low temperature would result in variants selection phenomenon and facilitate the formation of certain bainite variants  [24] .

Fig. 8 
                       shows the comparison of strength and ductility values of the advanced steels with similar chemical composition obtained by employing other thermomechanical treatments, including direct isothermal holding  [25–27] , two-step isothermal holding  [28] , grain refinement  [20,29] , external magnetic field  [30] , prior martensite  [31,32]  and prior ausforming  [17,20] . It is noteworthy that the present results achieved by ausforming for various strain level are located in the upper right of the strength-ductility map, which indicates that those processes exhibit superior strength-ductility combination than the above-mentioned methods.

Fig. 9 
                       shows the SEM morphologies of fracture surfaces in various tensile specimens. The fracture morphology of the non-ausforming sample mainly contains plenty of river-like quasi-cleavage facets mixed with tearing edges, indicating that the fracture manner is a mixture of quasi-cleavage fracture and ductile fracture mode, which implies the inferior tensile performance. However, the fracture surface of ausforming sample appears a large quantity of tearing edges and dimples, showing a typical ductile fracture characteristic, which is predominantly with ductile fracture, as evidenced by the tensile results of  Fig. 7 a.

Fig. 10 
                      a shows the hardness values of various specimens acquired with different ausforming processes. With increasing in ausforming strain, the hardness value increases progressively, and the maximum level can be achieved in the sample ausformed for 40% strain. In order to compare the dynamic impact and quasi-static tensile behavior of nanostructured bainitic steel with different ausforming strain, the impact energy and PSE are plotted in  Fig. 10 b. Obviously, the static and dynamic performances of nanostructured bainitic steel vary greatly under different ausforming strain. The quasi-static tensile property of ausforming samples outperform non-ausforming sample, whereas the impact toughness is evidently lower than the latter. With an increase of ausforming strain, the difference between dynamic impact and quasi-static tensile property is gradually magnified. The tensile strength and total elongation of ausforming samples both increase with strain, resulting in a noticeable enhancement in PSE compared to that of non-ausforming sample. On the contrary, the impact energy slightly enhances with increasing ausforming strain from 0 to 10%, then gradually reduces with further increasing strain to 40%. Thereinto, the sample processed by ausforming for 10% strain exhibits a maximum value of 31.2 J, which is much superior to the value of the ausforming sample with 40%, 12.1 J. These finds clearly indicate that a large ausforming strain immensely enhances the hardness and quasi-static tensile property of nanostructured steel, but worsens the impact toughness to a great extent.

Fig. 11 
                       shows the typical SEM fractography of impact fracture surfaces subjected to different ausforming processes. The fractography of non-ausforming sample consists of a large number of flat facets and a small quantity of large-sized dimples, implying that the fracture type is mainly quasi-cleavage fracture. However, in the ausforming sample with 10% strain, the apparent presence of finer dimples with less number of cleavage facets help to achieve the higher impact energy, which exhibits a mixed crack propagation mode of ductile fracture and quasi-cleavage fracture. Besides, with increasing in ausforming strain, a few number of fine dimples are present with quite a few cleavage facets, which indicates to be a typical quasi-cleavage fracture. Another striking feature is that plenty of cleavage facets and a small number of dimples appear to be distributed alternately in ausforming samples, resulting from the inhomogeneous plastic flow in individual austenite grain, which can be significantly distinguished in  Fig. 11 e.

sections.heading: Bainite transformation kinetics
paragraphs: As mentioned in the previous section, the incubation period and completion time of bainite transformation gradually shorten with increasing strain, but further marginally increase upon large deformation level, which suggests that the transformation kinetic changes non-monotonically with ausforming strain and the maximum degree of promotional function corresponds to the sample subjected to ausforming for 30% strain. These explanations for this trend may be closely associated with the processes of bainite nucleation and bainite growth  [33] . On the one hand, ausforming contributes to the increase of dislocation and vacancy, subgrain boundary and interface energy at grain interior, as well as grain boundary surface per unit volume by elongated austenite grains. These factors are all conducive to heterogeneous nucleation, which makes the nucleation position convert from prior austenite grain boundary to the blend of crystal defect and grain boundary, thus providing more nucleation sites for subsequent bainite reaction. Besides, the deformed storage energy in austenite generated by lattice distortion will reduce the nucleation driving force and impart additional driving force for bainite growth. Thereby, the bainite transformation can be definitely stimulated by ausforming process.

On the other hand, according to the ledge growth theory of bainite transformation, the growth rate of bainite lath is corroborated with carbon diffusion rate  [34,35] . Due to the formation of intense dislocation pile ups and sharp dislocation walls by large deformation, the diffusion of carbon atoms out from bainitic ferrite lattice to austenite encounters interruption, which retards the advance of glissile interface, involving displacive transformation from austenite to bainitic ferrite, and with increasing strain, the retardation effect of bainite growth becomes more severe. Moreover, the undercooled austenite can be strengthened by deformation, leading to a great resistance for bainite growth. Shipway also claimed that the bainite growth would be impeded by the dislocation debris once nucleated  [36] . However, a visible acceleration effect can be detected in this study with various ausforming strain, thus it can be concluded that the increase of nucleation sites plays a more critical role in bainite reaction. In terms of 40% strain, the promotion effect of facilitated nucleation can be counteracted by the inhibition effect of retarded bainite growth, resulting in an almost same transformation rate with the smaller strain. The results in present study are possible to identify the transformation kinetics resulted from ausforming in an attempt to reduce the duration of austempering and determine the optimum heat treatment process.

sections.heading: Microstructural morphology and phase component
paragraphs: From the microstructure observation, it can be recognized that the morphologies in ausforming samples have been significantly modified, which appears markedly discontinuous shape combined with more fragmented and shorter bainite sheaves in lieu of the typical sheaf-like structure in non-ausforming sample. This phenomenon may be attributed to the fact that the bainitic ferrite laths in non-ausforming sample dominantly initiate from the paraequilibrium nucleation of prior austenite grain boundary and grow in various directions, which causes the formation of a chaotic structure. However, for ausforming samples, carbon atoms will be segregated onto the crystal defect accumulated inside the broke parent austenite grains, leading to the regions close to defect possessing a high carbon concentration, and therefore, a corresponding carbon-depleted zone will be formed around them, which makes the bainite laths nucleate near the defects. Meanwhile, according to the perspective of shear mechanism  [37–39] , the growth of bainite lath cannot freely and continuously path through subgrain boundary, twin or dislocation cell, and hence bainite lath can be stifled as the advancing interface encounters crystal defect and limited in a single austenite grain. With increasing strain, the number of crystal defect increases, and the resultant growth space of bainite nuclei gradually decreases. These two factors control the bainite growth and bainite lath size, bringing about a short and broken bainite morphology. As a consequence of the irregular distribution of deformation band of undercooled austenite after ausforming, the formed bainite lath tends to be disordered on spatial scales.

The refined plate thickness of ausforming samples as compared to that of non-ausforming sample should be ascribed to two main reasons. Firstly, related researches show that austenite strength is the most crucial parameter that determines the bainite plate thickness, which primarily arises from the more restricted motion of glissile interface of γ/α and the decreased critical nucleus size of bainitic ferrite by the stronger austenite  [40] . Meanwhile, the austenite strength can be notably enhanced by ausforming and by increasing ausforming strain as well, which brings about a refined bainite lath. Secondly, the enhancement of dislocation introduced into the undercooled austenite by increasing ausforming strain largely raises the amount of bainitic ferrite nuclei, thereby further refining bainite sheaves. Given that the filmy retained austenite is isolated by the neighbouring bainitic ferrite plates, the finer plates lath accompanies slender thickness of austenite films  [41] . Besides, ausforming can reduce the number of bainite variants in an individual austenite grain, leading to the decrease of blocky retained austenite proportion, which in turn refine the final microstructure. Meantime, the variant selection becomes stronger with an increasing in ausforming strain, which can result in a reduction in blocky retained austenite fraction and an increase in interlath filmy retained austenite.

Compared to non-ausforming sample, ausforming process produces a small amount of bainitic ferrite formed in the final microstructure. This can be explained that the eventually obtained bainitic ferrite fraction generally relies upon nucleation density, growth rate and the average volume fraction of bainite sheaves generated from a single nucleus  [42] . According to above discussion, with the increase of ausforming strain, the increased crystal defect served as nucleation sites imparts more heterogeneous nuclei, which in turn increases the quantity of terminal bainite content. Nevertheless, the most of ausforming-introduced high-density dislocation debris and subgrains in parent-phase austenite may act as barriers to meddle with the movement of transformation interfaces, although some other dislocations do act as nucleation positions, resulting in the occurrence of severe work hardening of austenite, which improves the hindrance of shear growth of austenite to bainite and enhances the incompleteness of bainite transformation. Meanwhile, the decreased bainite sheaves will bring about the impingement of fresh bainite lath with existed bainite subunit, subgrain boundary and deformation bands, finally inducing a minor quantity of bainite transformed from deformation austenite. Therefore, ausforming strain has a twofold effect on bainite transformation, i.e., accelerating nucleation and retarding growth. When the ausforming strain reaches to a certain critical value, the increased nucleation amount sufficiently can compensate the inhibition effect due to the decreased growth rate and average volume of bainite sheaves upon ausforming, as confirmed from the ausforming sample for less than 30% strain, where the amount of bainitic ferrite is consistent with the non-ausforming sample. By contrast, the growth of average volume of bainite sheaves plays a decisive role in determining the phase components in the course of austempering when the ausforming strain further increases to 40%. This may be rationalized for the initial increase and then decrease in volume fraction of retained austenite with increasing ausforming strain.

The limited crystallographic orientations may be related to the different plastic deformation structure of undercooled austenite prior to isothermal bainite transformation, which results in different operated slip system  [13] . Meanwhile, due to the varying degrees of plastic flow and irregular strain partitioning in individual austenite grain by different ausforming strain, the dislocation arrays arrangement tends to be aligned along limited direction, consequently leading to the propagation of bainitic ferrite along one, two or three directions among those of 12 possible variants.

sections.heading: Tensile properties
paragraphs: Ausforming can accelerate isothermal bainite transformation and tailor the morphology and microstructural constituent, which may consequently affect the resultant mechanical properties of nanostructured bainitic steel.

According to strengthening mechanism of bainite described by Bhadeshia, the yield strength of nanostructured bainite steel is contributed by the pure annealed iron, substitutional solution atoms, carbon content, density dislocation and thickness of bainitic ferrite  [43] . Due to the absence of substitutional elements partitioning during bainite transformation, the ausforming process does not alter the intrinsic strength of iron and solid-solution strength.

It is expected that the operative strengthening mechanisms of ausforming samples mainly stem from bainitic ferrite thickness and dislocation density  [44] , namely the yield strength is proportional to the inverse of effective plates thickness and dislocation density. As increasing in ausforming strain, the significantly refined bainite lath, which can be clearly found in  Fig. 6 , decreases the mean free path for dislocation glide, resulting in grain refining strengthening. Meanwhile, the introduced dislocation in undercooled austenite by ausforming can be taken over by bainitic matrix and retained austenite at subsequent isothermal transformation, which plays an important role in dislocation strengthening, leading to the distinct enhancement of yield strength  [44] . Therefore, it is reasonable to expected that the YS should be continuously increased with increasing ausforming strain owing to the reduced bainitic ferrite lath thickness as well as the increased dislocation density.

Consequently, the improved tensile strength of ausforming process can be a direct consequence of grain refinement strengthening and dislocation strengthening together with strain-induced strengthening. The low temperature ausforming with a large strain is a desired route to acquire ultrahigh strength bainitic microstructure and may be an efficient procedure to manufacture nanostructured bainitic steel.

sections.heading: Hardness
paragraphs: With respect to microhardness, compared with non-ausforming sample, while even with a decrease in the amount of harder phase bainitic ferrite, as relative to retained austenite, there is tendency for hardness improve with increasing ausforming strain. For instance, the ausforming samples for 40% strain with almost 9% less bainitic ferrite, but the hardness increases from 500 HV of non-ausforming sample to 603 HV, which is increased by 22%. It has been reported that, similar to strength properties, the increased hardness value of nanostructured bainitic steel also originates from the ausforming-induced increase in dislocation density and microstructural characteristics correlated with bainite plate thickness  [50] , which can compensate the reduced bainitic ferrite volume fraction. The finer bainite plate and the higher dislocation density lead to higher hardness values.

sections.heading: Impact property
paragraphs: The distinct fracture mode of various samples can be directly related to the microstructural constituents and morphologies. As mentioned previously, comparing with thinner nanosized retained austenite, the microscale blocky retained austenite is more prone to rapidly convert into carbon-enriched, brittle martensite in the initial impact deformation process, which will absorb less impact energy and be conducive to crack tip initiation due to its lower resistance  [51,52] . Meanwhile, the newly transformed martensite may provide an easy fracture path for micro-crack propagation during impact loading, which is detrimental to toughness. Therefore, decreasing the dimension of blocky retained austenite as much as possible is of great benefit to avoid toughness degradation. Fortunately, ausforming can effectively increase the content of filmy retained austenite, playing a positive role in enlarging impact damage resistance via crack passivation, stress release and martensite transformation at the crack tip, which has been also reported that the well-known TRIP effect of moderately stable austenite underwent in impact process contributes to toughness improvement  [53] .

However, the effect of not only morphology but also the presence of crystal orientation of bainite sheaves on impact toughness behavior should be taken into account. As already reported in much other literature  [54,55] , bainitic ferrite lath with various crystallographic orientations can improve impact toughness by frequently deflecting crack propagation path and effectively increasing the resistance of crack growth. Conversely, the apparent variant selection brought about by ausforming will accelerate the crack propagation rate, and hence the increased degree of impact property can be partially counteracted by variant selection. Thus, it has a contradictory correlation between microstructural refinement and variant selection in ausforming samples. If the contribution value of refined microstructure is greater than that of variant selection, the decreased impact toughness in nanostructured bainitic steel due to the reduced variant number will be compensated, which consequently causes the impact performance of sample subjected to ausforming for a small strain (10%) to be better than that of non-ausforming sample. This finding seems non-consistent with the argument reported by Avishan, who proposed that ausforming for10% strain resulted in impact toughness declination  [19] . It may be attributed to different chemical composition and transformation time. Otherwise, further increasing ausforming strain, the promotion effect of refined bainite plates is diminished when the variant selection acts as a dominant position, especially, in the case of 30% and 40% strain, which consequently leads to comparatively low energies absorbed.

It is critical to note that ausforming with various strain seems to be an effective method not only in increasing the overall bainite transformation rate but also in improving tensile properties. However, only a relatively small amount of ausforming strain assists in the impact toughness improvement of nanostructured bainitic steel, while the increased strain will result in the deterioration of impact property. Therefore, great care must be taken into account the effect of strain levels on impact toughness.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs:
The role of undercooled austenite performed with various ausforming strain levels in isothermal bainite transformation behavior, microstructural evolution and strengthening-toughening mechanism of nanostructured bainitic steel has been broadly evaluated, and the corresponding results are enumerated below: 
                         
                            (1) 
                            Ausforming at 300 °C leads to lower necessary transformation hold time, which provides an effective method to decrease the time for producing nanostructured microstructure. However, the transformation rate depends on the applied strain level, with increasing strain up to 30%, the acceleration effect gradually enhances, but further slightly decreases after the larger deformation level. 
                         
                         
                            (2) 
                            Ausforming strain noticeably affects the volume fractions and morphologies of microstructural constituents, with increasing ausforming strain, the lower amount of bainitic ferrite, slighter austenite blocks, finer and shorter bainite plates, as well as limited crystal orientation can be achieved. 
                         
                         
                            (3) 
                            Ausforming strain has a positive effect on bulk hardness and tensile properties, which gradually increase as ausforming strain increases from 0 to 40%, yet only a relatively small amount of ausforming strain (10%) assists in the impact toughness improvement, the increased strain will result in the deterioration of impact property owing to the presence of strong variant selection. 
                         
                         
                            (4) 
                            The nanostructured bainitic steel obtains the optimal tensile properties of yield strength of up to 1550 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 1900 MPa and total elongation in excess of 24% with ausforming at 300 °C for 40% strain due to grain refinement strengthening and dislocation strengthening together with strain-induced strengthening.
